items.stem: Briefly explain why waste generation per person tends to increase with income.
items.answer: Higher incomes bring greater consumption of packaged goods, electronics, clothing and convenience food, more disposable products and shorter product lifespans; urbanisation adds packaging and less home composting.

items.stem: Briefly describe Copenhill (Amager Bakke), Copenhagen and explain what it reveals about incineration with energy recovery.
items.answer: A waste-to-energy plant opened in 2017 burns about 440,000 t of waste a year, supplying electricity and heating to about 150,000 homes. Burning residual waste provides energy and reduces landfill, though it still emits CO₂ and depends on a steady waste supply.

items.answer: Design for recyclability (single-polymer packaging); reuse and refill systems; extended producer responsibility; deposit-return schemes; reducing single-use plastic.

items.stem: Suggest how a landfill site could be managed to reduce its environmental impact.
items.answer: Impermeable clay/plastic liners and leachate collection; methane capture for energy; daily soil cover; compaction; groundwater monitoring; restoration as parkland after closure.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Waste generation is a problem caused mainly by high-income countries."
items.answer: High-income countries generate the most per person and have exported waste, but rapid growth elsewhere makes waste a global problem.

items.answer: municipal solid waste (MSW)

items.answer: anaerobic digestion

items.stem: Distinguish between reuse and recycling.
items.answer: Reuse uses a product again in the same form (refillable bottles), saving almost all the energy of making it; recycling breaks materials down to make new products, which requires energy and may reduce quality.
items.markingKey: Reuse uses a product again in the same form (refillable bottles), saving almost all the energy of making it; recycling breaks materials down to make new products, which requires energy and may reduce quality. items.stem: Explain why e-waste is both a hazard and a resource.
items.answer: It contains toxic lead, mercury, cadmium and flame retardants that pollute soil and water when dumped or burned (Agbogbloshie, Ghana); it also contains gold, copper, cobalt and rare earths - "urban mining" can recover them.

items.stem: Explain the environmental impacts of poorly managed landfill.
items.answer: Leachate contaminates groundwater and rivers; methane contributes to climate change and can cause explosions or fires; odour, vermin and disease; land take; plastics blown into the environment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Leachate contaminates groundwater and rivers; methane contributes to climate change and can cause explosions or fires; odour, vermin and disease; land take; plastics blown into the environment. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the linear economy and the circular economy.
items.answer: The linear economy follows take-make-dispose, generating waste at the end of each product's life; the circular economy designs products to be reused, repaired and recycled so materials circulate and waste is minimised.
items.markingKey: The linear economy follows take-make-dispose, generating waste at the end of each product's life; the circular economy designs products to be reused, repaired and recycled so materials circulate and waste is minimised. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: State two differences between biodegradable waste and non-biodegradable waste.
items.answer: Biodegradable waste (food, paper) is broken down by decomposers and can be composted but produces methane in landfill; non-biodegradable waste (most plastics, glass, metals) persists and must be reused, recycled or disposed of.
items.markingKey: Biodegradable waste (food, paper) is broken down by decomposers and can be composted but produces methane in landfill; non-biodegradable waste (most plastics, glass, metals) persists and must be reused, recycled or disposed of. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Outline why composting is considered a sustainable waste option.
items.answer: It diverts organic waste from landfill (avoiding methane), returns nutrients and organic matter to soil, reduces the need for fertiliser and is low-cost and possible at household or community scale.
items.markingKey: It diverts organic waste from landfill (avoiding methane), returns nutrients and organic matter to soil, reduces the need for fertiliser and is low-cost and possible at household or community scale. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of incineration and landfill for a city with little available land.
items.answer: Incineration: small land area, 90% volume reduction, energy recovery; but high cost, emissions and ash. Landfill: cheap but needs land the city lacks, methane, leachate. Incineration (with recycling) is likely more suitable, as in Singapore and Tokyo.

items.stem: Outline how extended producer responsibility encourages a circular economy.
items.answer: Producers pay for collection and recycling, so they have an incentive to design products that last, use less packaging and are easier to recycle (e.g. EU WEEE directive for electronics).
